title: Inclusive Teaching — Additional Needs

pts: Design flexible materials and tasks from the outset, benefiting all learners, not only those with identified needs.
Multiple means of representation, action and engagement reduce the need for individual retrofitting later.
This reframes inclusive design as good general design, not a separate, additional layer of work.
points.who: CAST's Universal Design for Learning framework

items: Take a lesson you are about to teach.
Check representation: is the key content available in more than one form (spoken, written, visual, physical)?
Check action and expression: can learners show what they know in more than one way (speaking, writing, drawing, acting, pointing)?
Check engagement: is there some choice, some relevance and some variation in pace?
Add one option under each heading where there is none.
Work with a colleague and plan one UDL-informed lesson together each month.
Start with one heading only if planning time is short; representation is usually the easiest to add.

blocks.x: A vocabulary lesson on weather, planned with UDL in mind:

lines: Representation: word + picture card + gesture + the word said aloud.
Action and expression: learners can say, write, draw or mime the weather.
Engagement: learners choose a city and describe today’s weather there.

blocks.x: None of these options is special to learners with additional needs. All of them help a mixed class.

body: Purpose: to summarize the three UDL principles. Content: a door with three entrances labelled ‘Ways to take it in’, ‘Ways to show it’ and ‘Ways to care about it’, with different learners (one with a hearing aid, one using a wheelchair, one with a book) using different doors into the same room. Style: warm, inclusive, no labels on the learners. Board version: three arrows pointing into one box.

items: CAST UDL Guidelines website (free), for the full checklist.

blocks.x: A three-column planning box in the lesson-plan template.

pts: Clear fonts, reduced text density, multi-sensory input and extra processing time support dyslexic learners without singling them out.
These adjustments are low-cost to implement for the whole class and rarely disadvantage anyone else.
Frame adjustments as standard classroom practice rather than visible individual accommodation where possible.

items: Take a crowded worksheet you use regularly.
Change the font to a clear sans-serif, at least 12–14 point.
Increase line spacing and leave more white space; use left alignment, not justified text.
Break long instructions into numbered steps, one action per step.
Replace italics or underlining for emphasis with bold.
Print on cream or pastel paper if possible, and give the whole class the new version.
Add a picture or icon beside each instruction.
Record the reading passage so learners can listen while they read.
Support: allow extra time and fewer items, with the same level of challenge in each item.
Challenge: not needed; the new format helps everyone.

lines: Read the passage carefully and underline all the verbs in the past tense and then write them in the table below together with their base forms and then use three of them in sentences of your own.
1. Read the passage.
2. Find the past tense verbs. Circle them.
3. Write them in the table.
4. Choose three. Write your own sentences.

blocks.x: Guidance such as the British Dyslexia Association’s Dyslexia Style Guide recommends clear fonts, generous spacing and avoiding dense blocks of text (British Dyslexia Association 2023 [VERIFY edition]).

body: Purpose: to show a worksheet makeover. Content: two versions of the same worksheet side by side: the first crowded, small, justified, with long instructions; the second spacious, with numbered steps, icons and a clear font. Style: realistic; no brand fonts named. Board version: not applicable.

items: Microsoft Word or Google Docs (free), with style templates set up once.
Immersive Reader in Microsoft tools (free), which reads text aloud and adjusts spacing.

blocks.x: Handwritten worksheets can follow the same rules: large, well-spaced writing with numbered steps.

pts: Short, varied tasks with clear structure and built-in movement breaks manage attention more effectively than long, single-format activities.
This aligns naturally with young-learner pacing principles from Unit 16, even in classes without a formal diagnosis.
Predictable routines (Unit 7) reduce the cognitive load of simply tracking what happens next.

items: Plan the lesson in chunks of 5–10 minutes, each with a different format.
Show the plan on the board as a simple list or icons.
Build in a short movement break between chunks (stand up and answer, a TPR task, move to a new partner).
Give one instruction at a time, and check it before starting.
Tick off each stage on the board as it ends.
Give one learner a job (handing out cards, holding the timer) that involves purposeful movement.
Support: seat learners who are easily distracted near the teacher and away from doors and windows.
Support: allow a fidget object that is silent and does not distract others.

lines: 1. Song ✓
2. New words (pictures)
3. Stand up: find a partner
4. Speaking game
5. Write three sentences
6. Goodbye
T: First, we listen. Then we stand up. Show me: first? (Ss point to ‘listen’.)

body: Purpose: to show chunked lesson structure. Content: a horizontal timeline broken into coloured blocks of different lengths, each with a small icon (ear, pencil, running figure, speech bubble), with a small arrow for ‘now’. Style: bright but uncluttered. Board version: a numbered list with ticks.

items: Online timers such as classroomscreen.com (free tier).

blocks.x: A sand timer or a clapping pattern for transitions.

pts: Clear sightlines to the teacher's face, visual instructions, and captioned audio or video are baseline accommodations.
Facing the class when speaking, rather than the board, matters more than most teachers initially assume.
This connects directly to Unit 7's guidance on supplementing spoken instructions with visual ones.

items: Seat the learner where they can see your face and the board, and ideally other learners’ faces.
Face the class when speaking; stop talking while you write on the board.
Write key instructions and new words on the board.
Use captions for any audio or video; if none exist, give a transcript.
Repeat learners’ answers so everyone hears them.
Check with the learner privately what works best for them.
Teach a few signs for common classroom instructions to the whole class. Where learners use Indian Sign Language, invite them to teach signs to the class if they wish.
Support: pair the learner with a partner who can share notes.

blocks.x: A short routine for listening tasks:

lines: Before: key words on the board.
During: audio with captions, or learner follows a transcript.
After: answers written on the board, not only said aloud.

body: Purpose: to show good seating and teacher positioning. Content: a classroom plan from above, with dotted lines showing a clear sightline between a learner near the front and the teacher’s face; a second small panel shows the teacher facing the board with a cross over the speech bubble. Style: simple plan diagram. Board version: not applicable.

items: YouTube automatic captions (free), checked for accuracy.
Live Transcribe on Android (free), which turns speech into text.

blocks.x: Printed transcripts and written instruction cards.

pts: Larger print, audio alternatives, and describing visual content aloud make materials genuinely accessible.
Any activity relying on unlabelled colour-coding or fine visual detail needs a non-visual equivalent path.
Check materials for this before the lesson, not as an improvised fix once a gap becomes visible.

items: Before the lesson, check every visual element: pictures, charts, colour codes, board diagrams.
For each, ask: could a learner who cannot see this still take part?
Add a spoken description or a tactile version (raised lines, objects).
Replace colour-only coding with labels or shapes as well.
Provide enlarged print or an audio version of reading texts.
Invite learners to describe pictures aloud for the class as a speaking task. This helps everyone.
Support: Braille materials where the learner reads Braille; coordinate with the school’s special educator.

blocks.x: Instead of ‘Look at the red words’, say:

lines: The words in red, the ones with a line underneath, are the new words: ‘harvest’, ‘festival’, ‘lamp’.
In this picture, there’s a market. On the left, a woman is selling vegetables. On the right, a boy is holding a kite.

body: Purpose: to show non-visual equivalents. Content: a colour-coded chart beside the same chart with shapes and labels (circle, square, triangle), and a small icon of a speech bubble describing it. Style: accessible design, high contrast. Board version: shapes drawn beside coloured words.

items: Screen readers such as NVDA (free, Windows) or TalkBack (free, Android).
Google Lookout (free, Android), which describes images and text aloud.

blocks.x: Real objects and raised-line drawings (glue lines on card).

body: About 8 per cent of men and 0.5 per cent of women of Northern European descent have some form of colour vision deficiency, most often difficulty telling red from green (Birch 2012). Rates vary between populations, but in any large class, at least one learner may not see a red–green code. Using labels as well as colours costs nothing.

pts: Additional needs describe how a learner best accesses learning, not a fixed ceiling on what they can achieve.
Framing accommodations as access, not remediation, changes both teacher expectation and learner self-efficacy (Unit 22).
The aim of an accommodation is equal access to the same challenge, not a lowered one.

items: Collect phrases you have heard (or used) about learners with additional needs.
Sort them into ‘deficit’ and ‘access’ language.
Rewrite the deficit phrases in access language.
Discuss how each version might affect a teacher’s expectations and a learner’s confidence.
Review a school report or record form for its language.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: ‘He’s weak in reading’ → ‘He reads more accurately when he has extra time and larger print.’
‘She can’t concentrate’ → ‘She works best in short tasks with movement breaks.’
‘Give them an easier test’ → ‘Give them the same test with extra time and a reader.’

blocks.x: The third example shows the key point. An accommodation changes the route, not the destination. This matters for self-efficacy (Unit 22): learners who are given the same challenge, with fair access to it, learn that they are capable.

body: Purpose: to illustrate access, not lowered expectation. Content: one mountain with the same summit flag; three paths lead up it, one with steps, one a ramp, one a winding trail, each used by a different climber. Style: hopeful, simple. Board version: a triangle with three lines to the top.

items: None needed; this is a reflection task.

pts: Where formal plans exist, the classroom teacher's role is to implement specified accommodations consistently.
Diagnosis and formal planning sit with specialists; consistent classroom implementation sits with the teacher.
Consistency across lessons matters as much as the accommodation itself — an inconsistently applied plan loses much of its value.

items: Read the learner’s plan and list the classroom accommodations it specifies.
Turn the list into a short checklist for your planner.
Before each lesson, check the list; after, tick what you did.
Share the checklist with any other teacher who teaches the learner.
Note what seems to help and report it at review meetings.
Where no formal plan exists, agree two or three simple accommodations with the learner and parents and follow the same routine.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: ☐ Seated near front, facing teacher
☐ Instructions written on board
☐ Extra 10 minutes for written tasks
☐ Reading text given the day before

blocks.x: An accommodation used on Monday and forgotten on Thursday tells the learner it cannot be relied on. Consistency builds trust.

body: Purpose: to show a simple implementation record. Content: a small grid with four accommodations down the side and the days of the week across the top, with most boxes ticked. Style: clean, practical. Board version: not applicable.

items: A shared Google Sheet (free) among the learner’s teachers.

blocks.x: A printed checklist kept in the teacher’s planner.

points.sub: Knowing the limit of general practice
pts: Recognise the limits of general classroom accommodation and know when to involve learning-support specialists.
Escalating appropriately is part of good inclusive practice, not an admission that general strategies have failed.
This keeps the teacher's role realistic and sustainable rather than solely responsible for every need in the room.

items: When you have concerns about a learner, record specific, dated observations (what you saw, in which task).
Note what you have already tried and the result.
Speak to the learner’s parents or carers and, where possible, the school’s special educator or head.
Share your observations; avoid naming a condition.
Continue your classroom support while the referral is made.
Keep a simple school-wide referral form so all teachers use the same process.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: 12 July: In copying from the board, R. often reverses ‘b’ and ‘d’ and misses lines. Reads aloud slowly but answers oral comprehension questions well. Tried: larger print, a ruler to follow lines. Some improvement with larger print.

blocks.x: Model language for speaking to parents:

lines: I’ve noticed that Riya understands a lot when we talk, but reading and copying take her much longer than others. I’d like us to find out more about how she learns best.

body: Purpose: to show the referral process. Content: three linked circles: an eye (‘Notice’), a notebook (‘Record’), two people talking (‘Refer’), with a loop arrow back to ‘Support in class’. Style: calm, supportive. Board version: not applicable.

items: Check what support your state or district provides, such as resource teachers under Samagra Shiksha [VERIFY local provision].

blocks.x: A paper observation notebook with one page per learner of concern.

body: Take your next worksheet and apply the makeover in point 2 before you use it. Give the new version to the whole class. Ask learners afterwards which version they find easier to read. The answer is often ‘the new one’, from almost everyone.

dek: Unit 23 of 100: designing classroom practice that works for learners with dyslexia, ADHD, or sensory impairment — often improving the class for everyone else too.

aims.x: This unit looks at how the English classroom can work for learners with additional needs, including dyslexia, attention difficulties and sensory impairment. The central argument is simple: most changes that help these learners also help everyone else.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain the principles of Universal Design for Learning;
adapt materials and tasks so they are dyslexia-friendly;
structure lessons that support learners who find sustained attention difficult;
make lessons accessible to learners with hearing or visual impairment;
use language that describes access rather than deficit;
implement an individual plan consistently;
recognize when a learner needs specialist support, and how to seek it.

why: Why this matters. Foundations built for an imagined 'typical' learner leave real learners with additional needs underserved. Inclusive design from the start, not retrofitted, closes that gap.

background.x: In any class of forty, some learners will find reading unusually hard, some will struggle to sit still and focus, and some will not hear or see the board as clearly as the teacher assumes. Many of these learners will never have been formally identified. The English teacher is not a diagnostician and should not try to be one. But the teacher does decide how a worksheet looks, how instructions are given, how long a task lasts and where learners sit. These decisions make a lesson easier or harder to access.

Two ideas shape current thinking. The first is Universal Design for Learning (UDL), developed by CAST, which asks teachers to build flexibility into lessons from the start rather than adding adjustments afterwards (CAST 2018). The second comes from research on language learners with specific learning differences. Judit Kormos and Anne Margaret Smith (2012) show that learners with dyslexia can and do learn additional languages successfully when teaching is structured, multi-sensory and explicit, and when they are given time.

India’s legal and policy framework supports this direction. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 recognizes specific learning disabilities, as well as hearing and visual impairment, and requires inclusive education in schools (Government of India 2016). The National Education Policy 2020 gives a whole chapter to equitable and inclusive education, and calls for teachers to be prepared to support learners with disabilities within regular classrooms (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020: ch. 6). The practical question is what that looks like on a Tuesday morning in Class 6.

items: Same test, fair access. Offer approved accommodations (extra time, a reader, larger print, oral responses) so the test measures English, not access.
Multiple ways to show learning. Where the aim allows, accept spoken, drawn or acted evidence as well as written work.
Progress over time. Compare each learner with their own earlier work, not only with the class.
Accessibility check. Review each test paper against the worksheet checklist before it is printed.
Which learners in your class might be struggling for reasons you have not yet noticed?
Which of your routine materials would fail a learner who could not see colour, or could not hear well?
What language do you and your colleagues use to describe learners with additional needs?
How consistently do you apply accommodations that have been agreed?
Who in your school or district can you turn to for specialist advice?

terms.def: The degree to which a lesson, material or test can be used by all learners, including those with sensory, physical or learning differences, through choices such as clear print, spoken instructions and flexible seating.

(1) An adjustment to how a learner accesses a task or test, such as extra time or enlarged print, which changes the route but not the destination. (2) In ELF talk, adjusting one’s speech to be understood by a listener.

Learning needs beyond those of most classmates, arising for example from dyslexia, attention difficulties or sensory impairment; changes that help these learners, such as clear routines and uncluttered worksheets, usually help the whole class.
Describing learners in terms of what they lack rather than what they can do or need; for example, ‘weak learners’ rather than ‘learners who need more time’.

A specific learning difficulty that mainly affects accurate and fluent word reading and spelling, despite adequate teaching and ability. Learners benefit from multisensory phonics, extra time and teaching that does not depend on reading instructions alone.
A written plan for a learner with special educational needs, setting specific goals, support strategies and review dates, agreed with parents and specialists.

The formal process of passing concerns about a learner to a specialist, such as a special educator, counsellor or medical professional, for further assessment and support. Classroom support should continue while the referral is being made.

A difference in the way a person processes information that affects particular aspects of learning, such as reading, spelling or number, without reflecting general intelligence. Dyslexia is the most familiar example.

A framework for planning lessons that are accessible to all learners from the start, by offering multiple means of engagement, representation and action and expression, rather than adapting afterwards for individuals.
